701.title: The second arrow
701.hook: the first arrow is pain; the second is our reaction to it (Samyutta Nikaya 36.6)
701.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the two arrows to describe how the mind adds suffering to pain, and meditators practice noticing bodily sensation directly while letting the added commentary pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first truth, a plain list, and your line was name it first. Did something go wrong that you gave a plain name before you fixed it? Today, what happens right after the naming. Day seven hundred one.

A dark kitchen, a glass of water, no lights on. A bare foot meets the leg of a chair, hard. That's the first part, and it's sharp, and it's real. Then the second part arrives, about half a second later. Who moved this chair. Why does this always happen to me. I can't even get a glass of water. Now the toe hurts, and so does the whole night. Often, what keeps us awake is the second part. A short teaching of the Buddha has a name for each of them. It calls them arrows.
screen: `A BARE FOOT, A CHAIR LEG.` → `THEN, HALF A SECOND LATER…` → `TWO ARROWS.`

segments.voice: First, same pain, two people. In the Samyutta Nikaya there's a teaching called the Arrow. The Buddha says that an untaught person and a trained disciple both feel things: pleasant, painful and neither. Pain comes to both. The difference is what happens next. When the untaught person is touched by pain, the text says, he sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast and becomes distraught. Second, one arrow, then another. It's like this, the Buddha says. A man is struck by an arrow, and then struck by a second arrow right after it. Now he feels the pain of two. The first is the pain in the body. The second is the pain the mind adds: the sorrowing, the lamenting, the beating of the breast. Third, some second arrows look like comfort. Then the text adds something. It says that the untaught person, touched by pain, goes looking for sense pleasure, because he knows no other way out of pain. So a second arrow isn't always a rant. Sometimes it's the snack, the scroll, the drink, reached for so that the first arrow doesn't have to be felt. Fourth, the first one still hurts. The trained disciple, the Buddha says, feels the first arrow and not the second. Bodily pain, yes. The added layer, no. This isn't a promise of numbness. The toe still throbs. The body still hurts. What drops away is the extra wound we fire into ourselves. This arrow, by the way, isn't the poisoned arrow from the parable we heard back in year one. Different teaching, same honesty about pain.
screen: `SAME PAIN, TWO PEOPLE.` · `ONE ARROW, THEN ANOTHER.` · `SOME SECOND ARROWS LOOK LIKE COMFORT.` · `THE FIRST ONE STILL HURTS.` · then, large: `SKIP THE SECOND ARROW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and wait for something slightly uncomfortable to show up. It will: an itch, a stiff shoulder, a sound you don't like, a worry drifting in. When it comes, find the first arrow. Just the plain sensation. Then watch for the second, the commentary that arrives right behind it: ugh, not this, why now. You don't have to stop it. Just notice it as a second arrow, and come back to the first one, which may be smaller than it seemed. Do this as many times as it comes. The bell holds the time.
The second arrow: in the Buddha's teaching, the pain the mind adds to the pain that comes. The first arrow is felt; the second is fired by us. Today's word.
Your line: skip the second arrow. Today, when something stings, catch one second arrow as it flies, the rant or the reach for comfort, and let the first arrow be enough. Day seven hundred one.

options: you feel nothing at all
you feel the bodily pain, but not the added sorrow

fork.reveal: one arrow, not two: the disciple feels bodily pain without the second, mental wound.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm person doesn't feel pain.
what it means: everyone is hit by the first arrow; the trained mind stops firing the second into itself.
what a scholar hears: Samyutta Nikaya 36.6, the Sallatha Sutta, where the untaught person feels two feelings, bodily and mental, and the instructed disciple feels only the bodily one.

702.title: The thirst
702.hook: the second truth: suffering comes with craving (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
702.howItsDone: Buddhists study the second noble truth as part of the four noble truths, and in meditation practice noticing craving as it arises, without acting on it or suppressing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two arrows, the pain that comes and the pain we add. Your line was skip the second arrow. Did you catch one in flight? Today we look at what keeps the bow drawn. Day seven hundred two.

Drink salt water and you get thirstier. The very thing you reach for to fix the thirst feeds it. Other things work a bit like that. One more episode, and the next one starts on its own. One more look at the phone. One more thing in the cart. Each one is supposed to settle it, and each one leaves the wanting a little wider than before. The Buddha's first teaching, after it names suffering, names where suffering comes from. And the word it uses is a word for thirst.
screen: `SALT WATER MAKES YOU THIRSTIER.` → `ONE MORE, AND ONE MORE.` → `A WORD FOR THIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Pali it's tanha, and the Pali-English Dictionary glosses it as thirst, and as craving. The same word does for a dry throat and a restless mind. Second, now here, now there. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the second noble truth says suffering arises with craving: a craving that is bound up with delight and passion, seeking delight now here, now there. That's the restlessness of it. It doesn't settle on one thing and rest. It finishes one glass and looks for the next. Third, three thirsts. The same teaching names three kinds. A thirst for sense pleasures: tastes, sounds, touch, the good things. A thirst for being: to become something, to last, to be someone. And a thirst for not being: for something to stop, to go away, not to exist. That third one is easy to miss. Pushing away can be thirst, too. Wanting the feeling gone, the person gone, the day over, has the same dry, reaching quality as wanting more. Fourth, not every wish. Tanha doesn't mean wanting anything at all. The Buddha's own path asks for effort, and when a teaching on right effort describes the wish for wholesome states, it uses a different word, chanda. That wish isn't called thirst. The thirst is the grasping kind of wanting: the kind that can't stand still, and never quite says enough.
screen: `TANHA: THIRST.` · `NOW HERE, NOW THERE.` · `THREE THIRSTS.` · `NOT EVERY WISH.` · then, large: `THE THIRST.`

segments.voice: Give it a moment of stillness. Before long a pull will turn up. To check something, to move, to get up, to make this end. When you notice it, don't feed it, and don't fight it either. Just look at it like thirst. Where is it in the body? The chest, the hands, the jaw? How strong, on a small scale? Then stay, and watch what it does when it isn't fed. It may grow for a moment. It may fade, and come back. You're only watching. The bell holds the time.
Tanha: Pali for thirst, the craving the second noble truth names as where suffering comes from. For pleasure, for being, and for not being. Today's word.
Your line: the thirst. Once today, when you reach for one more of something, pause with your hand halfway, and ask: is this thirst? Then choose. Day seven hundred two.

703.title: Only by love
703.hook: hatred never ends by hatred, only by love; this is an old law (Dhammapada 5)
703.howItsDone: Buddhists read and recite the Dhammapada's verses, and loving-kindness meditation is one practice used to soften resentment toward people who have caused harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tanha, the thirst, now here, now there. Your line was the thirst. Did you catch your hand halfway to one more of something? Today, one thirst in particular: the thirst to get even. Day seven hundred three.

He said that. In that tone. In front of everyone. Hours later the scene is still running: once in the shower, once in the car, and each time the comeback gets sharper. By now the argument has lasted far longer in one head than it did in the room. The other person has probably moved on to lunch. The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, has this scene in its first chapter. It even gives the replay.
screen: `HE SAID THAT. IN THAT TONE.` → `REPLAYED IN THE SHOWER.` → `THE DHAMMAPADA KNOWS THIS SCENE.`

segments.voice: First, the replay. In Max Müller's old translation, verse three goes: "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me." In those who harbor such thoughts, the verse says, hatred will never cease. And verse four turns it round: in those who do not harbor them, hatred will cease. The verses aren't about the insult. They're about the sentence we keep saying to ourselves afterward. Second, hatred doesn't end hatred. Then comes verse five: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." This is an old rule, the verse adds. It reads like common sense, and it's hard to live. Hitting back can look like ending it. The verse says it's a way of keeping it going. Third, the Pali says non-hatred. Müller chose the English word love. The Pali word is averena, which means by non-hatred, by the absence of enmity. That's worth sitting with. The verse isn't asking you to feel warm toward the person who wronged you, not today anyway. It's asking you to stop adding fuel. Love, in this verse, can start as simply putting the replay down. Fourth, an old rule. That's what the verse calls it. Not a clever tactic for winning. Just how hatred works, the way fire works. Feed it, and it burns. Stop feeding it, and it goes down.
screen: `HE ABUSED ME, HE BEAT ME…` · `HATRED DOESN'T END HATRED.` · `THE PALI SAYS NON-HATRED.` · `AN OLD RULE.` · then, large: `ONLY BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small hostility in your life right now. Not the deepest wound; something manageable. A coworker's sharp email, a neighbor, a relative's comment. Notice your replay sentence for it, the he said, she did. Hear it once. Then, gently, don't say it again. Each time it starts up, let it trail off, the way you'd stop feeding a fire. You don't need to forgive or feel warm. Just don't add a log. Stay with the breath for the rest of the time. The bell holds the time.
Only by love: the Dhammapada's old rule, that hatred never ceases by hatred, only by love, or in the Pali, by non-hatred. Today's word.
Your line: only by love. Today, when one hostility comes back to mind, catch the replay sentence and don't finish it. One log not added. Day seven hundred three.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to people who hurt you.
what it means: hatred keeps going while we feed it, in the replay and the hitting back; it ends when we stop.

704.title: The mind leads
704.hook: all that we are is the result of what we have thought (Dhammapada 1)
704.howItsDone: Buddhists read the Dhammapada's opening pair of verses as a teaching on intention: the state of mind behind speech and action shapes what follows, and meditation is one way of watching that happen.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hatred ceases not by hatred but by love, or in the Pali, by non-hatred. Your line was only by love. Did you leave one replay unfinished? Today we go back to the verse that opens the whole book. Day seven hundred four.

Which came first this morning, the mood or the thought? A message from a friend sits unanswered for three hours. A thought arrives: they're annoyed with me. Nobody said so. But within a minute the shoulders are up, the coffee tastes flat, and someone at home gets a short answer they didn't earn. Then the friend replies: sorry, phone died. The mood had already done its work. The Dhammapada begins with this chain, in its very first verse, and it puts the mind at the front.
screen: `AN UNANSWERED MESSAGE.` → `A THOUGHT: THEY'RE ANNOYED.` → `THE MOOD DOES ITS WORK.`

segments.voice: First, a big English line. Max Müller's old translation of the first verse begins: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." It's a sweeping sentence. Second, the Pali is plainer. The verse opens with a few short words about the mind: states have mind as their forerunner, mind as their chief, and are made of mind. Mano pubbangama: the mind goes in front. That's where today's line comes from. The mind leads. It walks ahead, and what we say and do comes along behind it. Third, two pictures. The verse goes on: if someone speaks or acts with an evil thought, "pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage." The ox steps, and the heavy wheel rolls right over the same ground. And the second verse is the mirror: speak or act with a pure thought, and "happiness follows him, like a shadow that never leaves him." A wheel and a shadow. One grinds along behind you; one goes wherever you go, without any weight at all. Fourth, what it's about. Look at what these verses actually join together: a state of mind, then speaking or acting from it, then what follows. They aren't saying a gloomy thought makes it rain, or that someone ill thought their way there. They're about the short road from mind to mouth to hands. It's the road from the unanswered message: they're annoyed, then tight shoulders, then a short answer at home.
screen: `A BIG ENGLISH LINE.` · `THE MIND GOES IN FRONT.` · `A WHEEL, AND A SHADOW.` · `FROM MIND TO MOUTH TO HANDS.` · then, large: `THE MIND LEADS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath be easy. Then just wait for a thought. Any thought: a plan, a memory, a worry, a name. When one comes, don't follow it out the door. Stay put, and watch what it does to the inside of you. Does the chest tighten or soften? Does the face change? Does a mood start to gather around it? See if you can catch the moment the thought steps in front and the mood falls in behind. Then let it go, and wait for the next. The bell holds the time.
The mind leads: the Dhammapada's opening, that states of mind go first, and what we say and do follows like a wheel or a shadow. Today's word.
Your line: the mind leads. Once today, when a mood arrives, look one step back and find the thought that walked in ahead of it. Day seven hundred four.

trapdoor: what you thought: you are whatever you think, so think positive.
what it means: the mind goes first, and speech and action follow from it, with pain or happiness behind.
what a scholar hears: Dhammapada 1–2, 'manopubbangama dhamma, manosettha manomaya': states have mind as forerunner, mind as chief, are mind-made. 'All that we are' is Müller's rendering.

705.title: Patacara's grief
705.hook: Patacara loses her whole family in a day, runs mad with grief, and later becomes a respected teacher (Therigatha commentary)
705.howItsDone: Buddhists tell Patacara's story from the commentaries and read her verses in the Therigatha, the poems of the early nuns.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mind goes in front, and speech and action follow like a wheel or a shadow. Your line was the mind leads. Did you find the thought that walked in ahead of a mood? Today, a story from the early nuns. Day seven hundred five.

A daughter of a wealthy family in the city of Savatthi falls in love with a servant in her parents' house. They know her family will never allow it, so the two of them slip away and make a life somewhere poor and far off. In time, a child is born. She is expecting a second, and she wants to go home to her mother to give birth. So with her husband and her little boy, she sets out on the road back to Savatthi. Her name is Patacara, and this is the road where she loses everything.
screen: `A RICH GIRL AND A SERVANT.` → `THE ROAD HOME TO SAVATTHI.` → `PATACARA.`

segments.voice: First, one road, one storm, one river. The story is told in the old commentary on the poems of the early Buddhist nuns. On the road a great storm breaks, and her labor begins. Her husband goes to cut branches for a shelter, and a snake bites him, and he dies there in the brush. She gives birth in the rain. In the morning a river is in flood. She carries the newborn across first and lays him on the bank. Halfway back for her older boy, a hawk swoops down on the baby. She screams and waves her arms, and her older son, thinking she is calling him, steps into the river and is swept away. When she reaches the city, she learns that in the night her parents' house fell in the storm, and her parents and brother are being burned on a single pyre. Second, come back to yourself. The story says she lost her mind. Her clothes fell from her, and she wandered the streets, and people threw rubbish and drove her off. She came to the grove where the Buddha was teaching, and he said to her, in effect: sister, recover your mindfulness. And she did. Someone threw her a cloak. Third, her own poem. Patacara later became a nun, and verses under her name survive in the Therigatha itself. In them she is washing her feet, and watching the water run down the slope, and her mind gathers, the way a good horse is trained. Fourth, a teacher. Another text, the Anguttara Nikaya, names her foremost among the nuns who knew the discipline, the rules of the order. The woman who ran through the streets became the one others came to learn from. Her poem ends with a lamp. We'll get to the lamp tomorrow.
screen: `ONE ROAD, ONE STORM, ONE RIVER.` · `SISTER, COME BACK TO YOURSELF.` · `HER OWN POEM: WATER ON THE FEET.` · `A TEACHER OF THE DISCIPLINE.` · then, large: `SHE WALKED ON.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the story settle for a moment. Then bring to mind someone you know, or know of, who survived a great loss. A grandparent who buried a child. A friend after a divorce or a death. A neighbor who lost a home. Picture their face. Hold the size of what they carried, as much as you can know it. And notice that they kept going: they got up, they cooked, they went to work, maybe they even taught others. Let yourself honor that, quietly, without needing to say anything. The bell holds the time.
Patacara's grief: an early Buddhist nun who lost husband, children, parents and brother, came back to herself, and became a teacher of the discipline. Today's word.
Your line: she walked on. Today, tell one person who carried a great loss that you see what they've carried. A message is enough. Day seven hundred five.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: Patacara, the nun's name as it appears in the Therigatha.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad old story about a woman who lost everything.
what it means: a woman broken by grief comes back to herself, and later teaches others.
what a scholar hears: two layers. her own verses are in the Therigatha; the story of the road, the river and the pyre is told in the later commentary on it.

706.title: It can end
706.hook: the third truth: suffering can cease, what Buddhists call nibbana, a going-out like a flame
706.howItsDone: Buddhists study nibbana as the third noble truth, the ending of craving, and Buddhist schools describe it in different words; meditators practice letting craving cool rather than feeding or forcing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Patacara's grief, the road, the river, and the woman who came back to herself. Your line was she walked on. Did you tell someone you see what they've carried? Today, the lamp at the end of her poem. Day seven hundred six.

At the end of a long dinner, somebody leans over and blows out the candle. A thin line of smoke goes up, and then nothing. Where did the flame go? It didn't go to the kitchen, or out the window, or up to the ceiling. It just isn't burning anymore. The question sounds almost silly. But in the Buddha's teaching, it turns out to be a serious one. The third of his four noble truths is good news, and the word for it comes from a fire going out.
screen: `SOMEONE BLOWS OUT THE CANDLE.` → `WHERE DID THE FLAME GO?` → `THE THIRD TRUTH IS GOOD NEWS.`

segments.voice: First, the third truth. In the Buddha's first teaching, after naming suffering and naming its source, the thirst, he names this: suffering can cease. And it ceases, the text says, with the fading away and ending of that very craving, letting it go, being released from it. Not a new thing added. A thirst that stops. Second, the word. In Pali it's nibbana; the Sanskrit form is nirvana. The dictionary of the old Pali texts gives its plain sense as the going out of a lamp or a fire. A related word, nibbuta, means cooled, put out. So the picture isn't a bright new place. It's a fire that has stopped burning, and the heat gone out of it. Third, Patacara's lamp. Remember the end of her poem in the Therigatha. One evening, after watching water run down the slope, she takes a lamp into her room, sits on her bed, and draws out the wick with a needle. As the lamp goes out, her poem says, her mind was freed. In her poem, the lamp going out and the mind set free come in the same moment. Fourth, which way did the fire go? In another teaching, a wanderer named Vacchagotta keeps asking where an awakened one goes after death. The Buddha asks him back: if a fire burning in front of you went out, would you know it had gone out? Yes. And which way did it go, east, west, north or south? The question doesn't fit, says Vacchagotta. A fire that's gone out doesn't go anywhere. The Buddha doesn't answer with a map. He answers with a flame that has gone out.
screen: `THE THIRD TRUTH: IT CAN END.` · `NIBBANA: A FLAME GOING OUT.` · `PATACARA'S LAMP.` · `WHICH WAY DID THE FIRE GO?` · then, large: `IT CAN END.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle. Find one craving that's burning a little right now. It might be big or small: for praise, for quiet, for an apology, for this to be over. Picture it as a small lamp flame. Patacara didn't blow her lamp out; she drew the wick down. So on each out-breath, let the wick of this wanting sink a little lower. No snuffing it, no fanning it. Just a lower wick, and a smaller flame. It may not go out. See if it cools, even a little, and notice the dimmer, quieter room around it. The bell holds the time.
Nibbana: Pali, in Sanskrit nirvana, the going out of a fire. In the third noble truth, the ending of craving, and with it, suffering. Today's word.
Your line: it can end. Today, catch one wanting that ends on its own, an urge that passes, a worry that drops away, and notice the moment it goes out. Day seven hundred six.

screen: `DAY 706 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EIGHT PARTS OF A PATH.`

707.title: Eight parts of a path
707.hook: the fourth truth: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration
707.howItsDone: Buddhists study the noble eightfold path as the fourth noble truth; in daily life practitioners often work with one factor at a time, such as right speech or right livelihood, alongside meditation for effort, mindfulness and concentration.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nibbana, a flame going out. Your line was it can end. Did you catch one wanting that went out on its own? Today, the last of the four truths, and the end of the week. Day seven hundred seven.

Three truths in, a practical question shows up. Fine. Suffering has a plain name. The thirst behind it has been found. And it can end, like a lamp going out. So what happens on Wednesday morning, with the dishes and the commute and the email that needs answering? The Buddha's first teaching doesn't leave that hanging. Its fourth truth isn't another idea. It's a path. And the path comes in eight parts, most of which look a lot like an ordinary day.
screen: `THREE TRUTHS IN.` → `SO WHAT HAPPENS ON WEDNESDAY?` → `THE FOURTH TRUTH IS A PATH.`

segments.voice: First, a middle way. In the Samyutta Nikaya, before he names any of the four truths, the Buddha names two roads to avoid. One is chasing sense pleasures. The other is tormenting yourself. Both, he says, are unprofitable. Between them runs a middle way, and that middle way is this path. Second, the eight parts. Right view. Right intention. Right speech. Right action. Right livelihood. Right effort. Right mindfulness. Right concentration. Say them slowly and notice how few of them happen on a cushion. Speech is what comes out at the checkout. Action is what the hands do. Livelihood is how the rent gets paid. Third, a nun sorts them. In the Majjhima Nikaya, a layman puts questions to the nun Dhammadinna, and she answers him. One answer groups the eight into three. Speech, action and livelihood belong to virtue. Effort, mindfulness and concentration belong to concentration. View and intention belong to wisdom. So the path has a shape: how you live with others, how you train the mind, and how you see. Fourth, one step at a time. Look back at the week. The second arrow and the thirst. Hatred that ends only by love, and the mind that leads. Patacara's grief and her lamp, and nibbana. All of that circled the first three truths: what hurts, where it comes from, and that it can end. The fourth truth is the one you walk. And nobody walks eight steps at once. A path of eight parts is still walked one step at a time, on one ordinary day, starting with whichever step the day hands you.

On the second time through, notice which one catches. Maybe speech, because of a conversation coming later. Maybe effort, because something has been put off. Let that one stay, and let the others rest. Then see where today will meet it: the room, the person, the hour. Just see it. The bell holds the time.
Eight parts of a path: the Buddha's fourth noble truth, the middle way, from right view to right concentration, walked in ordinary life. Today's word.
